This course introduces students to the theory and practice of visualizing data as both a research tool and communication strategy. The course is divided into two broad parts: data visualization and storytelling with visualizations.

In the first part of the course, we focus on how to create plots. This includes related topics such as data types and scale, tables and data frames, in addition to core Python visualization libraries, elementary and advanced plot types, and exploratory data analysis (EDA). The emphasis is on developing your media fluency to create the kinds of plots data scientists use in their work to understand and model data. We will also pause to survey some of the visualization techniques used for the broader world of data types you will encounter as a data scientist, including temporal, spatial, textual, and networked data.

In the second part of the course, we turn our attention to communicating the results of research through composition and storytelling. Here, the visualizations of the first part become the building blocks for creating presentations in various form, from static “infographics” to interactive visualization, in a variety of contexts, from scientific writing to journalism. Again, the focus is on developing your media fluency to create things. In addition, we develop our ability to critically examine how visual and narrative choices shape meaning and persuasion, and how to both avoid and detect misleading representations of data and findings.

Using plt.subplots() to control Pandas plots

[[Anatomy of a Figure]]

We start with a data frame that contains a nominal feature with unique values and an associated numeric feature.

This is the simplest form of data that can be visualized with a bar chart.

In this case, a bar chart will show us visually the differences in magnitude among the values A, B, an C for the nominal feature.
First, let’s acquire the data.

In this case, we’ll just make them up.

import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

my_data = [
	['A', 15],
	['B', 34],
	['C', 22]
]
df1 = pd.DataFrame(my_data)
df1



Before we plot anything, let’s properly label the axes in the data frame.

We will call the features F1 and F2.

It crucial that you label your data frames before you plot their since these labels will be used by the visualization tool.

df1.columns = ['F1', 'F2']
df1



Because the nominal data are unique, we can create a rudimentary bar chart just by converting the numeric value into a string.

for i, row in df1.iterrows():
    print(row['F1'], row['F2'] * '|')



We can improve the display by using the block character █ instead of a pipe:

for i, row in df1.iterrows():
    print(row['F1'], row['F2'] * '█')

Now, to produce this kind of chart we call Pandas’ .plot() method and pass it the argument kind = 'bar' along with passing features to the x and y axes of the plot.

df1.plot(kind='bar', x='F1', y='F2', title="A Very Simple Bar Chart")
plt.show()



Stop and inspect the resulting chart.

Question

Where did each of the elements of the data frame land on the chart?

Answer

F1 name \rightarrow x axis label

F1 domain \rightarrow x axis scale

F1 values \rightarrow positions of bars on x axis

F2 name \rightarrow the legend

F2 domain \rightarrow y axis scale

F2 values \rightarrow height of bars on y axis

Let’s clean the figure up a bit.

First, let’s remove the legend since it is not really needed in this example.

Second, let’s rotate the letters on the x axis for readability.

df1.plot(kind='bar', x='F1', y='F2', title="A Very Simple Bar Chart", legend=False, rot=0)
plt.show()



To create a horizontal chart, we set kind to barh.

df1.plot(kind='barh', x='F1', y='F2', title="A Very Simple Bar Chart", legend=False, rot=0)
plt.show()



Note that instead of using the argument kind, we can call bar and barh as chained methods to .plot(), like so:

df1.plot.bar(x='F1', y='F2', title="A Very Simple Bar Chart", legend=False, rot=0)
plt.show()

Note that if we do not set the value of x, Pandas will use the index as the x axis.

df1.plot.bar(y='F2', title="A Very Simple Bar Chart", legend=False, rot=0)
plt.show()



In fact, it is a good practice to assign the categorical feature to be the index in this case.

Since the values are unique, they can used as index values.

df2 = df1.set_index('F1')
df2.plot.bar(y='F2', title="A Very Simple Bar Chart", legend=False, rot=0)
plt.show()



Note also that if we pass a series to the plot method, by selecting a feature, we don’t need to specify the y argument either.

df2['F2']



df2['F2'].plot.bar(title="A Very Simple Bar Chart", legend=False, rot=0)
plt.show()



Tip

This is an important pattern to remember: selecting and shaping your data before visualization often makes the visualization code simpler.

In the preceding example we had a data set in which unique categorical feaatures are paired with numberic values.

In reality, we don’t often get data like this. More typically, the nominal values are repeated over observations.

Consider the Iris data set, which we will grab from the PyDataset library.

import pydataset

iris = pydataset.data('iris')
iris.columns = [col.lower().replace(".", "_") for col in iris.columns]
iris.sample(10)



Notice the repetition of the nominal feature species.

To plot this feature against any of the other numeric features, we need to group the other features by the nominal feature and grab an aggregate value, such as median, sum, or mean.

(
    iris.groupby(['species']).sepal_length.mean()
    .plot.bar(rot=0, title="Mean Sepal Length by Species")
)
plt.show()



Another thing we can do is just get the number of instances of a particular value in the nominal column.

iris.species.value_counts().plot.bar(rot=0)
plt.show()



Here we can see that the data set is balanced over species — there are 50 observations per species.

What if we want to compare the magnitudes of more than one numeric feature across a nominal feature, in this case species?

Let’s experiment to find out.

First, we get the mean of all the features by grouping on species and not specifying any columns to aggregate. Pandas will interpret this as saying you want all the columns aggregated.

Note that you should only do this if the columns are all numeric and come from the same domain.

iris_means = iris.groupby('species').mean()
iris_means



Now, when we call plot.bar(), Pandas creates a bar chart for each feature and then combines them.

By default, it combines them into groups.

iris_means.plot.bar(rot=0)
plt.show()



We can also combine them by stacking if we set stacked = True.

iris_means.plot.bar(rot=0, stacked=True)
plt.show()



Finally, we can use subplot = True to create a separate plot for each feature.

iris_means.plot.bar(rot=0, subplots=True)
plt.show()



Notice that this figure needs some work to improve its legibility.

Let’s change the size of the figure to give each plot more room.

To do this, we set figsize = (5,10), i.e. we set width to 5 and height to 10.

iris_means.plot.bar(rot=0, subplots=True, figsize=(5,10))
plt.show()

Finally, we can transpose the table to change the priority of categories.

The order of representation is as follows: Each observation row gets a bar, and each feature column gets a plot.

So, if we want each species to get its own plot with features as bars, we can use the .T operation to flip the table.

iris_means.T



iris_means.T.plot.bar(rot=0, subplots=True, figsize=(5,10), legend=False)
plt.show()



Of course, we can recreate the plots we made above with the new transposed table.

This plot shows the relative magnitudes of each feature over species.

iris_means.T.plot.bar(rot=0, stacked=True)
plt.show()

Pie charts are good for things like budgets, diets, etc., where there is a metaphorical pie that is divided into component parts.

Let’s create some imaginary data about someone’s nutrient consumption in the course of a day.

The numeric values are in grams.

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

my_data = {
    'protein': 65,
    'fat': 40,
    'carbs': 22
}
df = pd.Series(my_data)
df.plot.pie()
plt.show()

Let’s now look at a classic data set -- the Titanic data set.

This data set shows the survival rate of passengers on the ill-fated vessel that sank in 1912.

It consists entirely of nominal data for 1316 passengers.

These data are ideal for pie charts because:

Many features contains exhaustive and exclusive labels, meaning every passenger must belong to one and only category from each feature, e.g. class and sex.

The number of values per feature is small.

We can use pie charts to display each feature’s composition.

import seaborn as sns

titanic = sns.load_dataset('titanic')
titanic



titanic['age_group'] = np.where(titanic['age'] >= 18, 'adult', 'child')



We are only interest in a subset of categorial columns, so we select those.

my_cols = ['sex', 'age_group', 'class','survived']



titanic = titanic[my_cols]



titanic



Now let’s create a pie chart for each feature.

dfs = {}
for col in my_cols:
    dfs[col] = titanic.value_counts(col)
# titanic_vcs = pd.concat(dfs.values(), keys=dfs.keys(), axis=0)



for col in dfs:
    df = dfs[col]
    df.plot.pie(title=col.title(), figsize=(2,2))
    plt.show()









fig, ax = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(6,6))
for i, col in enumerate(titanic.columns):
    c = i % 2
    r = i // 2
    df = titanic.value_counts(col)
    df.plot.pie(title=col.title(), ax=ax[r,c])
plt.show()

We can see that there are two kinds of features in the Titanic data set: those that define the category of each person and one that defines the fate each person.

The first set may be thought of as input values and the second as the ouptput.

Let’s group the data by the category features and get the value counts of the survival feature. The produces a data frame where the categorical features form the index and the survival feature is projected onto the column axis.

titanic_vc = titanic[my_cols].value_counts().unstack(fill_value=0)
titanic_vc.columns = ['no','yes']
titanic_vc



In this form, the table tells us, “If a passenger was a first class adult male, what was their chance of surviving?”

We can use the survival rate data to compute a rough probability estimate as follows.

titanic_vc['total'] = titanic_vc['yes'] + titanic_vc['no']
titanic_vc['s_rate'] = round(titanic_vc['yes'] / titanic_vc['total'], 2)
titanic_vc.sort_values('s_rate')



Since these data are exhaustive, exclusive, and relatively few, we can use a pie chart to visualize the probabilities.

Note

Althought the categories are exhaustive and exclusive, the probabilities represented by the pie do not sum to 1. This is because each value is a joint probability for each combination of categorical features.

titanic_vc.s_rate.sort_values().plot.pie(title="Survual Rates")
plt.show()



How readable is this chart? Does it easily show which category combinations had the highest and lowest survival rates?

It turns out that pie charts become less useful as the number of categories increases.

In such cases, it is often better to fall back onto a bar chart.

The one below clearly shows which categories had the highest and lowest survival rates.

ax = titanic_vc.s_rate.sort_values().plot.barh()
plt.show()



Note

Be careful not to read too much into the survival rates of the first and second class children. Their total numbers are much smaller than the other categories.

Below, we visualize the fate of the adult passengers.

ax = (
    titanic_vc.query("age_group == 'adult'")
    .s_rate
    .sort_values()
    .plot.pie(title="Survival Rates of Adults")
)
plt.show()

Bar charts show numbers associated with the unique values of categorical features.

Pie charts show numbers associated with the unique values of categorical features where these values are exhaustive, exclusive, and relatively few.

Line charts allow us to visualize numeric data where the x axis consists of numerica data on an ordinal or ratio scale.

So far, we have looked at plots that involve categorical data.
Let’s look at a simple example.

Below, we visualize a small data set showing sales number over a series of years.

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

data = {
    'Year': [2021, 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025, 2026],
    'Sales': [100, 120, 170, 160, 210, 240]
}
df1 = pd.DataFrame(data)
df1



To create a line graph in Pandas, you can just call .plot() by itself. Line graphs are the default plot type.

In the example below, we set x to Year and y to Sales.

df1.plot(x='Year', y='Sales')
plt.show()



Of course, we can also call the .line() method explicitly.

df1.plot.line(x='Year', y='Sales')
plt.show()



Or we can set the kind argument to line

df1.plot(x='Year', y='Sales', kind='line')
plt.show()

In this example, we demonstrate how to plot more than one line in the same figure.

We create data showing number of units sold per month for two products, A and B..

data = {
    'Month': ['Jan', 'Feb', 'Mar', 'Apr', 'May'],
    'Product_A': [15, 20, 35, 30, 45],
    'Product_B': [25, 18, 22, 40, 48]
}
df2 = pd.DataFrame(data)

df2.plot.line(x='Month', y=['Product_A', 'Product_B'], title="Business is Booming")
plt.show()



Note

It makes sense to show multiple lines in the same figure if their associated features have the same domain.

In the example both lines represent prices of products.

We can show the two lines on separate axes with the subplots argument set to True.

df2.plot.line(x='Month', y=['Product_A', 'Product_B'], subplots=True)
plt.show()

As we saw earlier, Pandas defaults to showing the index of a data frame on the x axis if x is left unspecified.

Here we set Month to the index, since the values are uniqure over the observations.

Then, since the remaining non-index features are related, we don’t need to specify those, either. Pandas assumes you want to show them all.

df3 = df2.set_index('Month')
df3.plot()
plt.show()



df3.Product_A.plot.line(style='-o')
plt.show()



We can set the attributes of multiple lines by passing lists to the arguments.

df3.plot.line(style=['o-', 's--'], color=['blue', 'green'])
plt.show()



Note that these data can be visualized with a bar chart.

However, they are better visualized with a line graph to show the trend of the data over the numeric sequence.

df3.plot.bar()
plt.show()



Question

What differences do you notice in how the axes are represented?

Answer

The years on the x axis are treated as categories

The y axis is not clipped but begins with 0

Arbuthnot’s data describes male and female births for London from 1629-1710.

John Arbuthnot (1710) used these time series data to carry out the first known significance test. During every one of the 81 years, there were more male christenings (births) than female christenings. As Arbuthnot wondered, we might also wonder if this could be due to chance, or whether it meant the birth ratio was not actually 1:1.

Year:    The year, ranging from 1629 to 1710.

Males:   Number of male christenings (births).

Females: Number of female christenings (births).

Plague:  Number of deaths from the Plague.

Mortality: Total deaths (all causes combined) for that calendar year.

Ratio:   Ration of Males to Females.

Total:  The total number of births scaled in thousands (000s).

data_url = "https://vincentarelbundock.github.io/Rdatasets/csv/HistData/Arbuthnot.csv"
dfx = pd.read_csv(data_url)
dfx = dfx.set_index('Year')
dfx = dfx.drop("rownames", axis=1)
dfx.head()



dfx.plot(y='Total', style='.-', legend=False, title="Total Births per Year")
plt.show()



dfx.plot(subplots=True, figsize=(7.5,15))
plt.show()



dfx.describe().T

We two related features come from two domains, it becomes a problem when you try to show them on the same axes.

Matplotlib provides a function to solve this problem -- ax.twinx().

This function take an axes object returned by a Pandas plot an creates a new axes object that will be overlaid on the first, while using the right spine for the new domain.

ax = dfx.Total.plot(style='.-')
ax2 = ax.twinx()
dfx.Plague.plot(ax=ax2, color='orange', style='-')
plt.show()



dfx.Mortality.idxmax()

Line charts are also useful for plotting classicial mathematical functions, where y is a function of x, i.e. y = f(x).

df = pd.DataFrame()
df['x'] = np.arange(0, 5 * np.pi, 0.1)
df['sin_x'] = np.sin(df.x)
df.plot(x='x', y='sin_x')
plt.grid(True)
plt.show()



df['cos_x'] = np.cos(df.x)
df.head()



df.plot(x='x', y=['sin_x','cos_x'])
plt.grid()
plt.show()

Scatter plots are designed to show the relationship between two numeric features.

Specifically, they can show the covariance and correlation between numeric features.

When combined with categorical features, a scatter plot can show clustering.

Let’s generate some random numeric data

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns



df = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        'f1': np.random.randn(1000),
        'f2': np.random.randn(1000)
    }
)
df.head()



df.plot.scatter(x='f1', y='f2')
plt.grid()
plt.show()



Because these features are drawn from the normal distribution, they should exhibit not correlation.

Indeed, the result is a random blob of points that cluster around 0, the mean.

Let’s look at a more complex example.

penguins = sns.load_dataset('penguins').dropna()
penguins



penguins.plot.scatter(x='bill_length_mm', y='bill_depth_mm')
plt.show()



penguins.plot.scatter(x='bill_length_mm', y='bill_depth_mm', c='species')
plt.show()

pd.plotting.scatter_matrix(penguins, figsize=(10,10))
plt.show()

One limitation of a scatterplot is that it doesn’t do a good job of showing how many data points exists at a specific location.

The problem is called occlusion because some data point representations occlude others.

In the case of the Penguins data set, you can see that the three clusters have more points in their centroids, but it is not clear how many points are being covered up by other points.

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns

penguins = sns.load_dataset('penguins').dropna()

penguins.plot.scatter(x='bill_length_mm', y='bill_depth_mm')
plt.show()



One way to address the problem is to set the alpha parameter to a number less than 1.

In graphics lingo, the variable alpha \alpha stands for the color opacity of a visual element.

With a low alpha, stacked points appear darker because the colors of overlapping data points add up.

penguins.plot.scatter(x='bill_length_mm', y='bill_depth_mm', alpha=.3)
plt.show()



This is good, but we can do better.

Another approach is to divide the space into cells and color each cell as a function of the number of data points in the cell.

Pandas provides a .plot.hexbin() method that divides the space into hexagons and shades them by the concentration of data points.

penguins.plot.hexbin(x='bill_length_mm', y='bill_depth_mm')
plt.show()



To get the most out of this method, it is best to choose a gridsize value large enough to group a significant number of points in eache cell.

Here we use a value of 25.

penguins.plot.hexbin(x='bill_length_mm', y='bill_depth_mm', gridsize=25)
plt.show()



Finally, we can choose a color map that accentuates the distribution.

penguins.plot.hexbin(x='bill_length_mm', y='bill_depth_mm', gridsize=25, cmap="YlGnBu")
plt.show()



The resulting image is a kind of heatmap.

We’ll review these in a later chapter.

Let’s look at a data set with more occulusion.

The following data set for abalone -- a large sea snail with rich, flavorful meat -- is from the UC Irvine Machine Learning Repository.

According to the UCI site, the data set may used for [redicting the age of abalone from physical measurements.

Conveniently, the data are avaiable through a Python package ucimlrepo.

from ucimlrepo import fetch_ucirepo 
   
abalone_raw = fetch_ucirepo(id=1) 
abalone = abalone_raw.data['original']
abalone



We use a scatter matrix to find a candidate pair of features.

pd.plotting.scatter_matrix(abalone, figsize=(10,10))
plt.show()



From this, Diameter and Shell_weight look useful for demonstrating the value of a hexbin.

abalone.plot.scatter(x='Diameter', y='Shell_weight', alpha=.25)
plt.show()



Now, here is a hexbin version.

abalone.plot.hexbin(x='Diameter', y='Shell_weight', gridsize=25, figsize=(12,10))
plt.show()



The hexbin plot gives us a much better representation of the concentration of data.



Here is another pair of features.

abalone.plot.scatter(x='Shucked_weight', y='Rings', alpha=.25)
plt.show()



abalone.plot.hexbin(x='Shucked_weight', y='Rings', gridsize=25, figsize=(12,10))
plt.show()
